title: Epistaxis: first aid to escalation

guidelineVersions: GIRFT ENT Referral Guidelines (Adult), combined edition (published July 2025)
Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th edition (2023)

related.why: Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage: another ENT bleeding emergency with an escalation pathway
Stridor and upper airway obstruction: shares the A-E approach to an ENT airway emergency

brief.scenario: Mr Peter Langford, 58, has a persistent spontaneous nosebleed. He is sitting forward, repeatedly swallowing blood and becoming increasingly distressed.
brief.task: Assess the situation and explain your immediate management of significant epistaxis, including escalation if bleeding persists.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A-E first, then first aid technique and duration, then escalation thresholds, then the cautery decision.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating a normal blood pressure as reassurance to discharge, or cauterising blindly when no bleeding point is visible.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd assess him using an A-E approach, because significant epistaxis can cause airway compromise or haemodynamic instability."

flow: A-E assessment and immediate first aid

grid.label: Recognise major-haemorrhage risk (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Focuses only on the nosebleed itself, or lies the patient flat, without excluding airway compromise or haemodynamic instability.
grid.pass: Assesses using an A-E approach, recognising that significant epistaxis can cause airway compromise or haemodynamic instability.
grid.high: Checks specifically for posterior bleeding and airway-protection needs if the patient cannot manage swallowed blood, without letting the search for a bleeding point delay resuscitation.

grid.label: First-aid compression technique
grid.fail: Applies pressure to the nasal bones rather than the soft cartilaginous part, or repeatedly releases pressure to check within minutes.
grid.pass: Sits the patient forward, asks him to spit rather than swallow blood, and applies firm continuous compression to the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes without releasing early.
grid.high: States the pressure is held for a full 10 minutes and can be repeated up to twice before deciding it has failed, rather than checking sooner.

grid.label: Bleeding-risk history and access
grid.fail: Does not ask about anticoagulants, antiplatelets, bleeding disorders or previous epistaxis.
grid.pass: Reviews anticoagulants, antiplatelets, bleeding disorders and previous epistaxis, and obtains IV access and blood tests if bleeding is significant or the patient is unstable.
grid.high: Identifies the specific anticoagulant and its indication and involves the relevant specialist to balance bleeding risk, rather than stopping anticoagulation reflexively.

grid.label: Escalation threshold (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Repeats first-aid measures indefinitely, or discharges the patient because his blood pressure is normal despite ongoing bleeding.
grid.pass: Escalates severe bleeding that persists beyond 30 minutes despite conservative measures immediately to ENT on-call.
grid.high: Distinguishes urgent ENT referral for persistent bleeding from an immediate ED/on-call escalation when bleeding looks very severe.

grid.label: Cautery versus packing (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Performs, or says they would perform, blind cautery when no bleeding point is visible, or attempts cautery on both sides of the septum.
grid.pass: Only cauterises a clearly identified bleeding point; if the site cannot be seen, moves to packing or specialist referral rather than blind cautery.
grid.high: Explains that blind bilateral cautery risks septal perforation, so cautery is directed at one identified point at a time.

grid.label: Consider underlying pathology
grid.fail: Treats all epistaxis as self-limiting without considering red flags for recurrent or unilateral bleeding.
grid.pass: Considers an underlying sinonasal lesion in persistent unilateral or recurrent epistaxis and safety-nets accordingly.
grid.high: Arranges ENT follow-up specifically because of the unilateral, recurrent pattern rather than treating it as an isolated event.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd lie him flat and tell him to pinch his nose.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Where exactly, and for how long?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Wherever's easiest, and I'll check every couple of minutes to see if it's stopped.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Not really — I don't think his medications change what I do.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Bleeding continues despite this. What next?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Send him home if his blood pressure is normal.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: You cannot see a bleeding point. Would you cauterise?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd keep trying cautery on both sides until it stops.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, once it's stopped that's the end of it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd use an A-E approach, because significant epistaxis can cause airway compromise or haemodynamic instability.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you manage the bleeding itself?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd sit him upright leaning forward, ask him to spit rather than swallow, and apply firm continuous compression to the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes without releasing early.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd review anticoagulants, antiplatelets, bleeding disorders and previous epistaxis, and get IV access and bloods if bleeding is significant or he's unstable.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The bleeding continues despite this. What next?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If it's severe and persists beyond 30 minutes despite conservative measures, I'd escalate immediately to ENT on-call.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: You cannot see a bleeding point. Would you cauterise?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No — I wouldn't cauterise blindly without a visible bleeding point; I'd move to packing or specialist referral instead.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes — persistent unilateral or recurrent bleeding makes me think about an underlying sinonasal lesion, so I'd safety-net and arrange follow-up.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Given he's visibly distressed and swallowing blood, I'd take an A-E approach immediately, checking for posterior bleeding and whether he can protect his airway, without letting the search for a bleeding point delay resuscitation.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How exactly would you manage the bleeding?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sitting him forward so blood drains rather than being swallowed, asking him to spit, and holding firm compression on the soft cartilaginous part for a full 10 minutes without checking, repeated up to twice if needed before I decide it's failed.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Does anything in his history change your approach?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If he's anticoagulated, I'd identify the specific drug and indication rather than stopping it reflexively, and involve the relevant specialist to balance bleeding risk against why he's on it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Bleeding continues. What next, and how urgently?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Severe bleeding persisting beyond 30 minutes despite conservative measures needs immediate ENT escalation; if it looks very severe I'd go straight to the ED team rather than waiting to see if it settles.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Still no visible bleeding point. Cauterise?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No — blind cautery, especially on both sides, risks septal perforation. Without a visible point I'd move to packing and hand over to ENT for definitive control.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Anything else before this is finished?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Recurrent, unilateral bleeding like this makes me consider an underlying sinonasal lesion, so I'd arrange ENT follow-up rather than treat it as an isolated event, and document the anticoagulation discussion for whoever sees him next.

failures.move: Applying pressure to the nasal bones instead of the soft cartilaginous part.
failures.consequence: The compression does not occlude the bleeding vessels, so bleeding continues untreated.
Blood drains into the pharynx and can be swallowed or aspirated rather than draining out.

failures.move: Performing blind cautery, especially on both sides of the septum.
failures.consequence: Risks septal perforation without controlling a bleeding point that has never been identified.

failures.move: Discharging the patient because his blood pressure is normal despite ongoing bleeding.
failures.consequence: Normal observations can mask significant ongoing blood loss, delaying necessary ENT escalation.

recovery.when: You blank on what to do next
recovery.line: I'd like to structure this around immediate safety, assessment, escalation and definitive management.

recovery.when: Asked "anything else?" once bleeding has settled
recovery.line: Yes — I'd also consider an underlying sinonasal lesion, safety-netting and who else to inform.

knowledge.fact: Sit the patient forward and apply firm continuous compression to the soft cartilaginous part of the nose for 10 minutes, repeated up to twice if bleeding continues.
Severe epistaxis persisting beyond 30 minutes despite conservative measures needs immediate escalation to ENT on-call, or the ED team directly if very severe.
Blind random cautery is not performed when the bleeding point is not visible.
Persistent unilateral or recurrent epistaxis raises concern for an underlying sinonasal lesion and warrants ENT follow-up.

recall.think: Airway compromise or haemodynamic instability from major haemorrhage.
recall.say: "Significant epistaxis — assessing with an A-E approach while controlling the bleeding."
do: Sit forward, spit not swallow, compress soft nose for 10 min
A-E; IV access and bloods if unstable
Escalate to ENT on-call if persistent
recall.trap: A normal blood pressure does not mean it is safe to discharge ongoing bleeding.
recall.finish: ENT-directed cautery of a visualised point, packing, or surgical/interventional control.

partner.opening: Mr Peter Langford, 58, has a persistent spontaneous nosebleed. He is sitting forward, repeatedly swallowing blood and becoming increasingly distressed. "Assess the situation and explain your immediate management, including escalation if bleeding persists."

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about anticoagulants or bleeding history
reveals.finding: He takes an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation and has had two previous epistaxis episodes.
Bleeding slows during compression but restarts within a minute of release.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the bleeding site
reveals.finding: No bleeding point can be seen on anterior rhinoscopy.

push.question: Should the patient lie backwards?
push.expect: No — he stays sitting forward so blood drains out rather than into the pharynx or airway.

push.question: Can you cauterise both sides of the septum?
push.expect: No — cautery is directed at one identified bleeding point; blind bilateral cautery risks septal perforation.

push.question: The patient is anticoagulated. Do you stop everything immediately?
push.expect: Identify the anticoagulant and indication, assess bleeding severity, and involve senior/specialist clinicians rather than stopping automatically.

curveballs.prompt: The bleeding continues despite a full 10 minutes of pressure, repeated once.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Escalate — if it has been severe and persistent beyond 30 minutes despite conservative measures, refer immediately to ENT on-call.

curveballs.prompt: You still cannot see a bleeding point after resuscitation.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Do not perform blind cautery — proceed to packing or ENT referral instead.

curveballs.prompt: His blood pressure and heart rate stay normal throughout.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Normal observations do not exclude ongoing significant blood loss or the need for escalation if bleeding persists.

curveballs.prompt: He mentions several similar unilateral nosebleeds over the past few months.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider an underlying sinonasal lesion and arrange ENT follow-up rather than treating it as routine recurrent epistaxis.
